postbiotics-and-skin-microbiome.title: Postbiotics & the Skin Microbiome: What Fermented Cosmetic Ingredients Actually Do
postbiotics-and-skin-microbiome.excerpt: Fermented lysates, ferment filtrates, and prebiotic oligosaccharides dominate 2026 launches — but what does the evidence actually show? A mechanism-by-mechanism review of 12 microbiome actives against the ISAPP 2021 postbiotic consensus.
postbiotics-and-skin-microbiome.heroLead: From SK-II Pitera to La Roche-Posay's Bifidobacterium lysate, the cosmetic microbiome category is everywhere. Here is what the peer-reviewed evidence says — and where it still doesn't.

body.intro: Open any 2026 K-beauty or prestige derm launch and you will see the same vocabulary: postbiotic, microbiome, ferment filtrate, prebiotic, probiotic complex. The terms are used interchangeably in marketing copy, but in the underlying biology they describe four distinct things — and the difference matters for safety, formulation, and what an INCI list is actually telling you.
body.introThesis: The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) published a formal consensus definition of postbiotic in 2021[1], and that definition reshapes how we should read cosmetic labels carrying ingredients like BIFIDA FERMENT LYSATE, GALACTOMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE, or LEUCONOSTOC/RADISH ROOT FERMENT FILTRATE. This article walks through 12 of the most common microbiome-active cosmetic ingredients, what the peer-reviewed evidence says about each one, and how the INCI API scores them.
body.definitionsTitle: Probiotic, prebiotic, postbiotic — the ISAPP 2021 vocabulary
body.definitionsIntro: ISAPP's 2021 consensus separates three categories that the cosmetics industry has historically blurred:
body.definitionsProbiotic: Probiotic. A live microorganism that, in adequate amounts, confers a health benefit on the host. In food (yogurt, kefir, supplements) this is well-defined. In cosmetics it is almost never accurate — preservation systems and shelf-stability requirements kill live cells.
body.definitionsPrebiotic: Prebiotic. A non-digestible substrate selectively used by beneficial host or commensal microorganisms. In cosmetics: oligosaccharides like INULIN, ALPHA-GLUCAN OLIGOSACCHARIDE, and FRUCTOOLIGOSACCHARIDES. These feed resident Cutibacterium, Lactobacillus, and Staphylococcus epidermidis on the skin surface.
body.definitionsPostbiotic: Postbiotic. Per ISAPP: a preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host[1]. Critically, postbiotics are not live. They are heat-killed cells, lysates, cell-wall fragments, exopolysaccharides, organic acids, and secreted peptides.
body.isappCalloutBody: The ISAPP consensus locked in that postbiotic requires (a) inanimate microorganisms or their parts, and (b) a demonstrated health benefit. A simple bacterial fermentation by-product without efficacy data is not a postbiotic — it is a ferment metabolite. Almost every cosmetic ingredient marketed as "probiotic" is, in ISAPP terms, a postbiotic at best.[1]
body.liveProbioticsTitle: Why "live cosmetic probiotics" mostly don't exist
body.liveProbioticsBody: Cosmetic emulsions ship with broad-spectrum preservatives (phenoxyethanol, benzyl alcohol, sodium benzoate, organic-acid blends) that hold microbial growth under USP <51> and ISO 11930 challenge thresholds. A live Lactobacillus cannot survive a system designed to kill Staphylococcus aureus. The handful of products that genuinely deliver live cells (e.g. Mother Dirt AO+ Mist) avoid preservatives entirely, ship refrigerated, and carry short expiries. Everything else carrying "probiotic" on the front of the bottle is, by ISAPP's definition, a postbiotic.
body.lysateVocabTitle: Ferment, lysate, filtrate — the vocabulary trap
body.lysateVocabBody: INCI naming distinguishes three closely related preparations that the wider category often conflates. A ferment is the raw fermentation broth (cells plus medium). A ferment lysate is the same broth after physical or chemical disruption of cell walls, releasing intracellular fragments. A ferment filtrate is the supernatant after cells are removed by filtration — secreted metabolites and exopolysaccharides without intracellular content. BIFIDA FERMENT LYSATE and BIFIDA FERMENT EXTRACT share microbial origin but carry different fractions, and they score slightly differently on our safety scale.
body.microbiomePrimerIntro: Three facts about the skin microbiome are load-bearing for everything that follows.
body.residentTransientBody: The skin surface carries a stable resident community — dominated by Cutibacterium acnes in sebaceous areas, Staphylococcus epidermidis and S. hominis across most of the body, and Malassezia yeasts on the scalp and upper torso — overlaid with a constantly shifting transient population picked up from clothing, surfaces, and other humans[9]. Cosmetic ingredients can either reinforce the resident community (prebiotics feed commensals, postbiotic fragments stabilise immune tone) or perturb it (broad-spectrum antimicrobials, surfactant overuse, harsh acids).
body.phSebumBody: Healthy skin sits at pH 4.5–5.5. Resident Lactobacillus and Staphylococcus spp. tolerate this; transient pathogens including S. aureus grow optimally above pH 6. The resident community produces lactic acid and short-chain fatty acids that maintain the acidic skin film — this is competitive exclusion. Surfactant-heavy cleansers transiently push pH above 7 and disrupt the resident community for hours.
body.tlrReceptorsTitle: Keratinocyte TLR2/4 and the DAMP→PAMP crossover
body.tlrReceptorsBody: Keratinocytes — the dominant cell type in the epidermis — express toll-like receptors TLR2 and TLR4 on their surface. These receptors evolved to detect bacterial cell-wall fragments (PAMPs: pathogen-associated molecular patterns) and to mount inflammation. Postbiotic lysates deliver the same molecular patterns (lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan, S-layer proteins) but at low, controlled doses, training the receptor without triggering a full inflammatory cascade. This is the mechanistic basis for ferment-lysate "soothing" claims — sub-threshold TLR ligation downshifts subsequent NF-κB and IL-1α release.
body.fermentLysatesTitle: Ferment lysates: bacterial fragments as topical messengers
body.fermentLysatesIntro: This is the most clinically validated of the four families. Heat-killed cell fragments survive cosmetic preservation systems intact, supply consistent doses of bacterial PAMPs, and have a 25+ year market and clinical history.
body.lactoBifidoBody1: LACTOBACILLUS FERMENT LYSATE and BIFIDA FERMENT LYSATE are the two anchor postbiotics in modern sensitive-skin formulations. Gueniche et al. ran a randomised double-blind vehicle-controlled trial of topical Bifidobacterium longum lysate (10% w/w in cream, twice daily, 2 months) on 66 women with reactive skin; the lysate arm showed a significant reduction in lactic-acid-sting score and improved barrier recovery compared to vehicle[2]. The same team's 2007 work on a Bifidobacterium ferment lysate in a UV-protection model showed reduced UV-induced minimal erythema dose change and accelerated repair of DNA-damage markers[3].
body.lactoBifidoBody2: Mechanistically, the active fractions are S-layer proteins, lipoteichoic acid, and lactic acid — all of which down-modulate IL-1α and IL-6 release by keratinocytes after sensory-irritant challenge. Both ingredients sit at safetyScore: 9 in INCI API: extensive market history, ISAPP-aligned postbiotic profile (no live cells), no published sensitisation flag.
body.galactomycesTitle: Galactomyces ferment filtrate (Pitera and the AhR pathway)
body.galactomycesBody1: GALACTOMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE is the backbone of SK-II's Pitera franchise (where it is used at 70–90% of the formula in the iconic Facial Treatment Essence). Mechanistically it is a yeast filtrate supplying vitamins (B1, B2, B6, biotin), amino acids, and pyruvate. Lee et al. (2017) characterised its molecular pharmacology and showed activation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathway in cultured human keratinocytes, with downstream upregulation of filaggrin and aquaporin-3[4]. Filaggrin is the central structural protein of the cornified envelope; aquaporin-3 governs glycerol and water flux into the epidermis.
body.galactomycesBody2: On the clinical side, a 4-week split-face trial of 90% Galactomyces ferment filtrate showed measurable improvement in skin radiance, hydration, and pore-area appearance vs vehicle[4]. We hold the safetyScore at 8 rather than 9 because the AhR pathway activation, while well-tolerated, is more pharmacologically active than a simple postbiotic lysate, and because yeast metabolite enrichment is a theoretical Malassezia-folliculitis flag (see caveats below).
body.lactococcusBody: LACTOCOCCUS FERMENT LYSATE (typically derived from Lactococcus lactis subsp. cremoris H61) is the best-characterised postbiotic in Japanese dermatology literature. Kimoto-Nira et al. ran a 4-month RCT in middle-aged women combining oral and topical L. lactis H61; the active arm showed improved skin moisture and reduced photo-ageing biomarkers[5]. The active fraction is a lactococcal exopolysaccharide that ligates TLR2 and downregulates IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α. INCI API rating: safetyScore: 8 — one tier below the more thoroughly studied Lactobacillus and Bifida lysates.
body.saccharomycesBody: SACCHAROMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE is a yeast filtrate supplying β-glucans, trehalose, and glutathione precursors. β-glucan ligates the dectin-1 receptor on keratinocytes and primes a mild innate-immunity tone associated with enhanced barrier recovery. Same safetyScore: 8, with a precautionary comedogenicityRating: 1 for fungal-acne-prone users (Malassezia cross-reactivity to yeast cell-wall fragments is debated).
body.vitreoscillaTitle: Vitreoscilla ferment — where the evidence is weakest
body.vitreoscillaBody: VITREOSCILLA FERMENT sits at the edge of the postbiotic category. Vitreoscilla is a Gram-negative microaerophilic bacterium whose haemoglobin (VHb) binds oxygen with very high affinity. Cosmetic claims center on "cellular oxygenation," and the underlying mechanistic literature on VHb in non-native hosts is real and indexed[12]. But the dermal-clinical evidence is industry-sponsored and largely unindexed in PubMed — there is no published vehicle-controlled RCT comparable to the lysate trials cited above. We score it at safetyScore: 7 and flag the efficacy evidence level as IN_VITRO.
body.prebioticSubstratesIntro: If postbiotics deliver bacterial fragments directly to the receptor, prebiotics take the indirect route: supply a selective carbon source that resident commensals can ferment but transient pathogens cannot. The clinical endpoint is a measurable shift in microbial composition toward commensal predominance.
body.inulinAlphaGlucanBody1: INULIN is a linear fructose polymer (β-2,1 glycosidic linkages) that is non-digestible in human cells but is selectively fermented by skin commensal Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium spp. The downstream metabolites — acetate, lactate, propionate — lower local pH and tilt competitive exclusion in favour of the resident community.
body.inulinAlphaGlucanBody2: ALPHA-GLUCAN OLIGOSACCHARIDE (commercial form: Bioecolia, Solvay) is a bio-enzymatic α-1,6-glucoside oligomer with degree of polymerisation 3–10, produced enzymatically from sucrose and maltose. Lambers et al. (2008) ran a 4-week split-face trial of 2% α-glucan oligosaccharide and reported a 1.7-fold shift in the resident:transient flora ratio measured by 16S sequencing[6]. Both ingredients sit at safetyScore: 9 with zero comedogenicity and no published irritancy flag.
body.fosBody: FRUCTOOLIGOSACCHARIDES are short-chain β-2,1 fructose oligomers (DP 2–9) derived from inulin hydrolysis or sucrose transfructosylation. Mechanistically identical to inulin at lower molecular weight, which means faster fermentation kinetics on skin. Bouslimani et al. (2019) used FOS-containing formulations in their landmark mass-spec/16S study of how cosmetic products reshape the skin microbiome and showed selective enrichment of S. epidermidis over S. aureus[14]. Same safety class as inulin: safetyScore: 9, GRAS food substrate, no topical-safety flag in 30+ years of market history.
body.synbioticStackingTitle: Why prebiotic + postbiotic is the formulation default in 2026
body.synbioticStackingBody: The pre-2020 cosmetic playbook layered a single fermented active. The post-ISAPP playbook combines them — "synbiotic" in nutrition terminology, prebiotic + postbiotic in cosmetics terminology[10]. A typical 2026 essence might pair BIFIDA FERMENT LYSATE (postbiotic, supplies the molecular signal) with INULIN + ALPHA-GLUCAN OLIGOSACCHARIDE (prebiotic, feeds the resident community that produces ongoing endogenous postbiotic metabolites). The combination is additive — the postbiotic supplies the immediate receptor ligation; the prebiotic sustains it.
body.naturalPreservationTitle: Natural preservation: Leuconostoc and the bacteriocin route
body.leuconostocChemistryTitle: Leuconostoc/radish root ferment filtrate — the bacteriocin chemistry
body.leuconostocChemistryBody1: LEUCONOSTOC/RADISH ROOT FERMENT FILTRATE (commercial: Leucidal Liquid) is the workhorse of natural-preservation systems in ECOCERT- and COSMOS-certified cosmetics. Chemically it is the filtrate of Leuconostoc kimchii fermented on radish root, dominated by leucocin-A family bacteriocins — class IIa antimicrobial peptides[15] — plus organic acids (lactic, acetic) at low pH.
body.leuconostocChemistryBody2: The bacteriocin spectrum is selective: it depresses Gram-positive pathogens (Listeria, S. aureus) while sparing commensal coagulase-negative staphylococci[7]. That selectivity is the marketing edge over phenoxyethanol or parabens — and the regulatory grey zone, because LEUCONOSTOC/RADISH ROOT FERMENT FILTRATE is not on EU Annex V (the preservative list); it functions as a conditioning agent with preservative side-action. Cosmetics Europe has published position papers debating where it belongs.
body.contactDermatitisTitle: Contact-dermatitis case reports — read the small print
body.contactDermatitisBody: Hougaard et al. (2021) reported a clean case series of allergic contact dermatitis attributed to LEUCONOSTOC/RADISH ROOT FERMENT FILTRATE in patch-tested patients[8]. The implicated antigen is most likely a bacteriocin peptide fraction rather than the radish-derived components. The case rate is low — much lower than methylisothiazolinone or formaldehyde-releasers in equivalent surveys — but non-zero, and our safetyScore: 8 (rather than 9) reflects this. Sensitive-skin profiles should treat it with the same precaution as any peptide-based natural preservative.
body.fungalAcneCalloutBody: GALACTOMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE, SACCHAROMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE, and other yeast-derived ferments enrich the formula with yeast metabolites and cell-wall fragments. In Malassezia-folliculitis-prone users (sometimes called "fungal acne"), high-percentage yeast ferments have been anecdotally associated with flare-ups. The clinical evidence is thin and inconsistent, but the precautionary stance in our database is comedogenicityRating: 1 for yeast ferments (vs 0 for bacterial lysates) and a textual note flagging the Malassezia question.
body.nonLivingBody: ISAPP's definition is deliberately strict on this point: postbiotics are <bold>inanimate</bold><sup>[1]</sup>. This matters for safety. Live cosmetic probiotics — if they existed widely — would carry colonisation risk, sepsis risk in immunocompromised users, and unpredictable interactions with the resident community. Postbiotic lysates and filtrates do not. There is no published case of cutaneous infection from a postbiotic cosmetic, and the ingredients are routinely used in atopic-dermatitis adjunctive therapy where barrier compromise is significant.
body.malasseziaTitle: Yeast-derived ferments and the Malassezia question
body.malasseziaBody: Malassezia species (M. globosa, M. restricta, M. furfur) are commensal yeasts that, under conditions of sebum overload or barrier disruption, can drive seborrhoeic dermatitis and Malassezia folliculitis. The theoretical concern with GALACTOMYCES and SACCHAROMYCES ferments is that yeast-derived β-glucans and cell-wall fragments could cross-prime the Malassezia population. The mechanistic evidence is weak but not zero. INCI API flags both ingredients with a non-zero comedogenicity rating and surfaces a textual notes field warning fungal-acne-prone users to patch-test.
body.soyPhytoBody: LACTOBACILLUS/SOYBEAN FERMENT EXTRACT is a K-beauty active in which Lactobacillus fermentation of soybeans liberates aglycone isoflavones — genistein and daidzein — from glycosylated precursors. Wang et al. (2014) showed a 22% MASI-score reduction in melasma over 12 weeks in a vehicle-controlled trial[13]. The downside: genistein and daidzein are weak phyto-oestrogens with measurable activity at oestrogen receptor β. The expected topical systemic dose is very low, but the INCI API default for this ingredient is pregnancySafe: null pending senior derm review, not true. Soy-protein-allergic users should patch-test.
body.apiScoringTitle: How INCI API scores these ingredients
body.apiScoringIntro: Our safety-scoring rubric for microbiome actives is anchored in three factors: (a) market history and exposure volume, (b) presence of vehicle-controlled clinical evidence, and (c) ISAPP-aligned non-living status. The result is a tight 7–9 band for the entire family — narrower than the spread for retinoids (3–7) or AHAs (5–8).
body.scoringBandsTitle: Why most postbiotics earn 8–9 on our safety scale
body.scoringBand9: Score 9 — heat-killed lysates with multi-decade market history and indexed vehicle-controlled clinical trials: BIFIDA FERMENT LYSATE, BIFIDOBACTERIUM LONGUM LYSATE, LACTOBACILLUS FERMENT LYSATE, plus the prebiotic substrates INULIN, ALPHA-GLUCAN OLIGOSACCHARIDE, FRUCTOOLIGOSACCHARIDES.
body.scoringBand8: Score 8 — postbiotics with shorter evidence base or a defensible caveat: GALACTOMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE (fungal-acne flag), SACCHAROMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE (same), LACTOCOCCUS FERMENT LYSATE (smaller clinical base), LEUCONOSTOC/RADISH ROOT FERMENT FILTRATE (contact-dermatitis case reports), LACTOBACILLUS/SOYBEAN FERMENT EXTRACT (phyto-oestrogen activity, null pregnancy stance).
body.scoringBand7: Score 7 — long market history but weak indexed clinical evidence: VITREOSCILLA FERMENT. Mechanism is biotech-grade and real; cosmetic-clinical RCTs are not published in indexed journals.
body.exampleResponseIntro: Querying the public API for any of the ingredients above returns the standard cosmetic-ingredient envelope. The fields below are the trimmed shape returned by GET /v1/ingredients/BIFIDA%20FERMENT%20LYSATE:
body.weakestEvidenceBody: VITREOSCILLA FERMENT and LACTOBACILLUS/SOYBEAN FERMENT EXTRACT are the two outliers. The Vitreoscilla mechanism (haemoglobin-mediated cellular oxygenation) is real in biotechnology contexts[12] but unproven in indexed dermal-clinical work. The soy-Lactobacillus extract has indexed RCT evidence[13] but introduces phyto-oestrogen activity that demands a precautionary pregnancy stance. Both are flagged with evidenceLevel: IN_VITRO in our efficacy seed and should be communicated to end users as "emerging" rather than "established" actives.
body.bottomLineTitle: Bottom line — which postbiotic actually belongs in your routine
body.bottomLineIntro: The microbiome category contains real science and real marketing in roughly equal measure. The evidence-weighted shortlist:
body.bottomLineSensitive: Reactive or sensitive skin: BIFIDA FERMENT LYSATE or BIFIDOBACTERIUM LONGUM LYSATE — strongest indexed RCT evidence for reduced sting and improved barrier recovery[2][3].
body.bottomLineDull: Dull or uneven skin: GALACTOMYCES FERMENT FILTRATE — clinical evidence for radiance and hydration via the AhR/filaggrin axis[4]. Skip if you have a documented fungal-acne pattern.
body.bottomLineBarrier: Barrier maintenance and microbiome support: A prebiotic + postbiotic stack — INULIN or ALPHA-GLUCAN OLIGOSACCHARIDE alongside a bacterial lysate. This is the 2026 formulation default for good reason[6][10].
body.bottomLineSkip: <bold>Probably skip:</bold> Anything sold as a "live probiotic cream" that is shelf-stable at room temperature in a standard cosmetic preservation system. By ISAPP's definition, no live organisms are surviving in that bottle<sup>[1]</sup>.
body.bottomLineOutro: And finally: the cosmetic microbiome category is a young one. The ISAPP consensus is from 2021; most of the indexed clinical evidence is post-2010. Expect the next decade to refine — not invalidate — the picture above as larger, longer, and better-controlled trials accumulate.

what-is-a-barcode.title: What Is a Barcode? UPC, EAN, GTIN and How Lookup Works
what-is-a-barcode.excerpt: A practical guide to the GS1 numbering system that powers every retail scanner on the planet — how UPC-A, EAN-13 and GTIN-14 are structured, how check digits work, and how INCI API resolves a barcode into a real cosmetic product.
what-is-a-barcode.heroLead: Every cosmetic SKU on a store shelf carries a globally unique number. Here is what that number actually encodes — and how we turn it into a full INCI analysis.

body.intro: If your app scans cosmetic products, the entire experience hinges on one small number on the back of the box. That number is a <bold>GTIN</bold> — a Global Trade Item Number — and it is managed by <gs1Link>GS1</gs1Link>, the non-profit that runs global barcode standards in 116 countries. Everything INCI API does starts there.
body.familiesTitle: The barcode families you'll actually see
body.familiesIntro: Retail barcodes come in four main flavours. They are not different standards — they are different lengths of the same GTIN namespace, padded with leading zeros when converted up.
body.familyUpc: <bold>UPC-A (GTIN-12)</bold> — 12 digits. The classic US and Canadian retail barcode. Every drugstore you've walked through in North America is running these.
body.familyEan13: EAN-13 (GTIN-13) — 13 digits. The dominant format everywhere else. A UPC-A is just an EAN-13 with a leading 0.
body.familyEan8: <bold>EAN-8 (GTIN-8)</bold> — 8 digits. Used for small packaging (think lipstick tubes) where a full-length barcode won't fit.
body.familyGtin14: <bold>GTIN-14 / ITF-14</bold> — 14 digits. Used on shipping cartons and cases, not consumer scans.
body.anatomyIntro: Take a real cosmetic barcode — 3600523217175 (L'Oréal Paris Revitalift serum):
body.anatomy1: Digits 1–3: GS1 country prefix. 360 is France. It tells you where the number was issued, not where the product was manufactured or sold.
body.anatomy2: <bold>Digits 4–7: Company prefix.</bold> Assigned by the national GS1 office to a single legal entity (e.g. L'Oréal S.A.).
body.anatomy3: <bold>Digits 8–12: Item reference.</bold> Allocated by the brand itself. One SKU, one variant, one specific formulation.
body.anatomy4: <bold>Digit 13: Check digit.</bold> A mod-10 checksum computed over the first 12 digits.
body.calloutPrefixTitle: Why country prefixes are often misread
body.calloutPrefixBody: A barcode starting with 690–699 was issued by GS1 China — but this only means the GS1 membership is Chinese. The product can be manufactured anywhere in the world. Never display a "made in" claim based on the prefix alone. INCI API returns country of issuance explicitly as prefixCountry so you don't confuse it with the manufacturing origin.
body.checkDigitIntro: The last digit of every GTIN is a self-correcting checksum. The algorithm is the same whether you're decoding a UPC-A or an EAN-13:
body.checkDigit1: Starting from the rightmost data digit, multiply alternating digits by 3 and 1.
body.checkDigit3: The check digit is the smallest number that makes that sum a multiple of 10.
body.checkDigitOutro: This catches ~90% of single-digit transcription errors and most adjacent swaps. If your scanner returns a GTIN whose check digit fails, reject it — it's almost always a misread, not a valid code you've never seen before.
body.lookupTitle: From a scanned number to a full INCI analysis
body.lookupIntro: When your app calls GET /v1/products/:barcode, INCI API does the following work, in order, behind a single HTTP response:
body.lookup1: Normalise the GTIN. UPC-A → EAN-13 by left-padding with 0. Check digit re-validated. Both forms indexed.
body.lookup2: <bold>Resolve the product</bold> from our MongoDB index of 450K+ cosmetic SKUs, merged from 2,400+ sources.
body.lookup3: <bold>Fetch cosmetics_details</bold> — the full INCI ingredient list, ordered by declared concentration.
body.lookup4: <bold>Run ingredient intelligence.</bold> For each INCI token we look up the cosmetic_ingredients collection: EU CosIng ID, CAS number, safety score, allergen status, comedogenicity, pregnancy flags.
body.lookup5: <bold>Aggregate.</bold> Per-product safety score (1–10), clean beauty score (0–100), allergen count, unsafe-during-pregnancy flag, per-skin-type compatibility.
body.lookup6: <bold>Respond.</bold> One JSON payload, P95 well under 300 ms when cached in Redis.
body.missingTitle: When a barcode isn't in the database
body.missingIntro: Cosmetics is a long-tail category — there are thousands of niche brands, regional variants, and limited-edition SKUs. Our coverage is strong but not infinite. When we miss, three things happen:
body.missing1: The parser-planner queues the unknown barcode for targeted link collection against our top universal fallbacks (UPCitemdb, EAN-Search, BarcodeSpider, GoUpc, Barcodelookup).
body.missing2: The parser-worker pool picks the task up from RabbitMQ within minutes, runs per-source circuit breakers and rate limits, and persists whatever normalized fields it finds.
body.missing3: End users on inciapi.com/checker can optionally submit a product URL — and every approved contribution flows into the same normalisation pipeline.
body.takeaway1: Treat UPC-A and EAN-13 as the same identifier. Always store the 13-digit canonical form.
body.takeaway2: Validate the check digit client-side before you call the API.
body.takeaway3: Don't infer product origin from the GS1 prefix — it tells you who issued the number, not who made the product.
body.takeaway4: For cosmetic SKUs, the barcode is only half the story. The real value is the INCI list behind it — and that requires a live, continually refreshed database. That's what INCI API is for.
body.calloutTryBody: Scan any cosmetic product and paste the barcode into our <checkerLink>public checker</checkerLink> — or hit the live endpoint in the <playgroundLink>Playground</playgroundLink>. Free for everyone right now: 20,000 requests per month, no credit card.

how-we-source-ingredient-data.title: Where INCI API Data Comes From — 2,400+ Verified Sources
how-we-source-ingredient-data.excerpt: A look inside our ingredient pipeline: 2,400+ brand and retailer sources, official regulatory databases (EU CosIng, FDA, Health Canada, ANVISA), automated freshness checks, and the safety graph built on top.
how-we-source-ingredient-data.heroLead: Trustworthy ingredient data is a sourcing problem before it is an API problem. Here is exactly where every field in the INCI API response comes from.

body.intro: An ingredient API is only as good as its sources. INCI API currently ingests from <bold>2,400+ distinct data sources</bold> spanning brand websites, retailer catalogues, regulatory databases, open scientific datasets, and user contributions. Every field we return is traceable back to at least one of them. This is how that pipeline is built.
body.tiersIntro: Not all sources are equal. We organise them into three tiers, and the tier controls freshness policy, conflict resolution, and confidence score.
body.tier1Intro: Authoritative, licensable, and structurally consistent. These define our cosmetic_ingredients collection — the safety graph.
body.tier1Cosing: <bold>EU CosIng</bold> (European Commission) — 30,000+ ingredients, CC BY 4.0. Provides INCI names, CAS/EC numbers, cosmetic functions, EU Annex status (II/III/IV/V/VI), max concentrations. <cosingLink>cosing homepage</cosingLink>
body.tier1EuReg: <bold>EU Regulation 1223/2009</bold> + amendment <bold>2023/1545</bold> — the legal source of truth for the EU 80+ mandatory fragrance allergen list we flag automatically.
body.tier1Fda: <bold>FDA VCRP & OTC Monographs</bold> — US regulatory status for colorants, sunscreen actives (21 CFR 352), and flagged ingredients.
body.tier1HealthCanada: <bold>Health Canada Cosmetic Ingredient Hotlist</bold> — prohibited and restricted substances under Canada's Food and Drugs Act.
body.tier1National: <bold>ANVISA (Brazil)</bold>, <bold>NMPA (China)</bold>, <bold>MHLW (Japan)</bold>, <bold>KFDA (Korea)</bold> — national cosmetic regulations used for regional compliance flags.
body.tier1Iarc: <bold>IARC Monographs</bold>, <bold>NTP RoC</bold>, <bold>California Prop 65 list</bold> — carcinogen classifications.
body.tier1Cir: <bold>CIR (Cosmetic Ingredient Review)</bold> — US expert panel safety assessments (open literature).
body.tier1Pubchem: <bold>PubChem</bold>, <bold>ChemSpider</bold> — chemical identity cross-references (InChIKey, SMILES) for disambiguating trade names.
body.tier2Intro: Large, crowdsourced, and structurally predictable. These provide our barcode-to-product backbone.
body.tier2Obf: <bold>Open Beauty Facts</bold> (ODbL) — ~200,000 cosmetic products with INCI lists, barcodes, imagery. Our single largest import.
body.tier2Makeup: <bold>MakeupAPI</bold> — ~900 makeup SKUs with shade/finish metadata, free tier.
body.tier2Wikidata: <bold>Wikidata</bold> (CC0) — brand ownership graph, parent companies, headquarters countries.
body.tier2Gs1: GS1 country prefixes — public table, used to populate prefixCountry at ingest time.
body.tier3Intro: The long tail. Direct brand e-commerce sites, national retailer chains, pharmacies, and K-beauty/J-beauty/halal-beauty specialty shops. Each one is a dedicated collector + aggregator pair, and each one is geographically targeted for language and INCI format.
body.tier3Brands: Brand sites — L'Oréal, Estée Lauder, Shiseido, Unilever, P&G, Johnson & Johnson portfolios, plus 1,500+ indie brands. Canonical source for current formulations.
body.tier3Retailers: <bold>Regional retailers</bold> — Sephora, Ulta, Douglas, Notino, Boots, Rossmann, DM, Watsons, Mecca, Iherb, Lyko, Etsy Beauty, plus category specialists.
body.tier3KBeauty: <bold>K-Beauty + J-Beauty ecosystems</bold> — Hwahae, Olive Young, Cosme (@cosme), Istyle, Cosmetic-Info-JP — with language-specific INCI extractors for Hangul, Kanji, and Hiragana/Katakana headers.
body.tier3Pharmacy: <bold>Pharmacy chains</bold> — dermocosmetic brands (La Roche-Posay, Eucerin, CeraVe, Avène, Vichy, Bioderma) via 300+ national pharmacy platforms.
body.pipelineTitle: The parser pipeline, end to end
body.pipelineIntro: Every source — tier 1 regulatory or tier 3 brand site — flows through the same two-service architecture:
body.pipeline1: parser-planner (singleton). Runs on a per-source cron stored in MongoDB data_source_configs. For each enabled source: discovers new URLs via sitemaps, category APIs, or direct catalogues; queues stale products for re-scrape; emits tasks to RabbitMQ.
body.pipeline2: parser-worker (replicated). Pulls tasks, selects the matching aggregator from our 2,400+ registry, enforces per-source rate limits via token buckets, wraps every fetch in a circuit breaker, and writes normalized output to products, cosmetics_details, or cosmetic_ingredients.
body.pipeline3: <bold>ingredient-service.</bold> Joins each new INCI token to the safety graph, computes aggregate scores, and materialises the response shape the API returns.
body.calloutScrapeTitle: Why copy-paste scraping doesn't work at this scale
body.calloutScrapeBody: Brand and retailer sites change templates constantly. Our abstract aggregator rotates realistic browser User-Agents, handles gzip sitemaps, follows robots-aware crawl rules, and falls back to headless Playwright for JavaScript-rendered pages. When a site moves from server-rendered to SPA, only the one affected aggregator breaks — not the pipeline.
body.freshness1: <bold>Content hashing.</bold> Every scraped page is hashed. If the hash hasn't changed since the last scrape, we skip re-processing — saves ~60% of worker CPU on returning crawls.
body.freshness2: Per-source stale threshold. Regulatory sources: monthly. Brand sites: weekly. High-churn retailers (Sephora new arrivals): daily. Configured per source in data_source_configs.staleThresholdDays.
body.freshness3: User-triggered refreshes. Any POST of a product URL to /v1/products/submit bumps that item to the head of the queue.
body.freshness4: <bold>Dead-letter queue.</bold> Transient errors (429s, timeouts) are retried with exponential backoff; permanent failures land in the DLQ for manual review.
body.qualityTitle: Data quality — what we do about it
body.qualityIntro: Scraped data is noisy. We learned this the hard way: in an April 2026 audit of 100 random products, we found ~30% of one source's entries were table headers mistaken for ingredient names, and another slice were marketing prose. Here is what now guards the pipeline:
body.quality1: <bold>Header blacklists</bold> per locale ("成分名", "INCI", "화장품 표시명", etc.) are rejected at extraction.
body.quality2: Prose detectors — if a token list reads like English sentences (attracts, helps, therefore), the aggregator returns empty and the product is queued for a better source.
body.quality3: <bold>Per-token validation</bold> — length, character set, and cross-reference against the known INCI vocabulary (~30,000 entries from CosIng).
body.quality4: Single write boundary. All inci fields go through one normalizer before touching MongoDB — guarantees every stored list is an array of clean strings.
body.transparencyIntro: We don't just return a scored result and ask you to trust us. Every product includes a dataSource: DataSourceType[] array listing every source that contributed, plus a qualityScore (0–100) that reflects completeness and agreement between sources. For ingredient lookups, the response carries per-field provenance:
body.licensingBody: We respect upstream licenses. EU CosIng is CC BY 4.0 — we attribute in our documentation. Open Beauty Facts is ODbL — same. Wikidata is CC0. Brand sites we crawl under the fair-use / normal-web-browsing terms they themselves publish in their robots.txt and ToS. Aggregated, transformed, scored output is our own product under the INCI API <licenseLink>license</licenseLink>.
body.calloutSupportTitle: Want data for a source we don't yet cover?
body.calloutSupportBody: Open a support ticket at <contactLink>inciapi.com/contact</contactLink> with the source URL. New aggregators take 1–3 days to land and start backfilling.

niacinamide-evidence-review.title: Niacinamide: Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence and Safety
niacinamide-evidence-review.excerpt: A reference review of niacinamide (vitamin B3) — ceramide biosynthesis, pigmentation, sebum regulation, and the clinical trials behind the 4–5% topical concentrations used in modern serums.
niacinamide-evidence-review.heroLead: Niacinamide is on almost every modern cosmetic label. Here is the actual peer-reviewed evidence — not the marketing copy.

body.intro: Niacinamide (nicotinamide, INCI NIACINAMIDE, CAS 98-92-0) is the amide form of vitamin B3. It shows up in virtually every modern cosmetic line — from $8 drugstore serums to $180 luxury moisturizers — and unlike many of its shelf-mates, the evidence behind it is real. This is a reference review of the peer-reviewed literature, not a marketing sheet.
body.mechanismIntro: Niacinamide is a precursor to two critical cellular coenzymes — NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ — which drive more than 400 enzymatic reactions, including DNA repair, energy metabolism, and reactive oxygen species defence. Beyond that, the topically relevant mechanisms break down into four buckets:
body.mechanismCeramide: <bold>Ceramide biosynthesis.</bold> Tanno et al. (2000) demonstrated in cultured human keratinocytes that nicotinamide increases ceramide content, free fatty acids, and cholesterol — the three components of stratum corneum intercellular lipids. This directly strengthens the skin barrier <sup>[1]</sup>.
body.mechanismPigmentation: <bold>Pigmentation modulation.</bold> Hakozaki et al. (2002) showed that niacinamide does not inhibit tyrosinase directly but instead blocks melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes — a 35–68% reduction in melanosome transfer in vitro, with corresponding clinical lightening in a 28-subject trial <sup>[2]</sup>.
body.mechanismSebum: <bold>Sebum regulation.</bold> Draelos et al. (2006) reported a statistically significant reduction in sebum excretion rate after 2–4 weeks of 2% topical niacinamide in Japanese and Caucasian subjects <sup>[3]</sup>.
body.mechanismAntiInflam: <bold>Anti-inflammatory activity.</bold> Niacinamide inhibits PARP (poly-ADP-ribose polymerase) and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokine release, which is the basis for its documented efficacy in rosacea and acne.
body.clinicalTitle: Clinical evidence — the trials that actually matter
body.ageingBody: The Bissett et al. (2005) split-face randomised controlled trial with 50 Caucasian women, 12 weeks, 5% niacinamide, is still the most frequently cited aging trial. Significant improvements over vehicle control were measured in fine lines/wrinkles, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness, yellowing (sallowness), and elasticity <sup>[4]</sup>.
body.melasmaBody: Navarrete-Solís et al. (2011) conducted a double-blind, randomised clinical trial comparing 4% niacinamide to 4% hydroquinone in 27 patients with melasma over 8 weeks. Both treatments produced significant improvement; niacinamide reached 44% "good-to-excellent" improvement vs 55% for hydroquinone, with significantly fewer side effects [5].
body.acneBody: Shalita et al. (1995) — topical 4% niacinamide gel vs 1% clindamycin gel, 8 weeks, 76 patients with moderate inflammatory acne. Both achieved comparable reduction in acne severity (52% vs 54% improvement) and inflammatory lesion count <sup>[6]</sup>. Niacinamide carries no antibiotic-resistance risk, which is why it remains a standard over-the-counter option.
body.rosaceaBody: Draelos et al. (2005) — 2% niacinamide moisturizer in 50 rosacea patients, 4 weeks, showed barrier improvement (TEWL reduction) and subjective symptom relief <sup>[7]</sup>.
body.cirBody: The Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel concluded that niacinamide is safe as used in cosmetic formulations at concentrations up to 10% (CIR Final Report, 2005; re-reviewed 2020). No evidence of carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, or sensitisation at topical concentrations.
body.euBody: Niacinamide is <bold>not restricted</bold> under Regulation 1223/2009. It does not appear on Annex II (prohibited), Annex III (restricted), Annex V (preservatives), or Annex VI (UV filters). It is freely usable in cosmetics sold in the EU, with no mandated maximum concentration.
body.fdaBody: FDA classifies niacinamide as GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) for dietary supplement and food use. In cosmetics, it is not scheduled — use is governed by general cosmetic safety requirements.
body.pregnancyBody: Niacinamide is widely regarded as pregnancy-safe. It is the form of B3 typically used in prenatal supplements. INCI API returns pregnancySafe: true for niacinamide with no dose cautions.
body.formulationTitle: Formulation notes — what brands get wrong
body.formulationPh: <bold>pH window.</bold> Niacinamide is stable between pH 5–7. Below pH 3.5 it hydrolyses to nicotinic acid, which causes flushing and irritation. This is why pairing a pure niacinamide serum with a pure vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid, pH ~3) serum at the same step can cause temporary redness — it's a pH incompatibility, not a chemical clash.
body.formulationConc: <bold>Concentration ≠ efficacy.</bold> Most trials showing benefit use 2–5%. Above 10% the marginal benefit is poorly demonstrated and tolerance drops sharply — tingling, flushing, and transient erythema become common.
body.formulationStable: <bold>Stable ingredient, stable product.</bold> Unlike retinol or vitamin C, niacinamide is resistant to oxidation, light, and heat. No opaque packaging required.
body.compatibilityIntro: Because niacinamide works on ceramides, sebum, and pigmentation simultaneously, it is one of the few actives that is genuinely broadly applicable. INCI API returns:
body.calloutQueryBody: GET /v1/ingredients/niacinamide/full returns the full 20-point profile used to generate this article. References and skin-type compatibility are in the response body.

retinoids-safety-and-pregnancy.title: Retinoids, Retinol and Pregnancy Safety — What the Evidence Says
retinoids-safety-and-pregnancy.excerpt: Retinoic acid, retinol, retinyl palmitate and HPR compared. Why systemic absorption matters, what the FDA and EMA say, and how we flag retinoids for pregnancy risk in the INCI API.
retinoids-safety-and-pregnancy.heroLead: Retinoids are the most studied — and most misunderstood — class in skincare. Here is what regulators actually say, and what the API returns.

body.intro: Retinoids are the single most clinically validated class of anti-aging ingredients in cosmetic science — and simultaneously the class with the clearest pregnancy contraindications. Understanding which retinoid you have in a product, what concentration, and what the systemic absorption profile looks like is the difference between a safe recommendation and a teratogenic warning.
body.familyIntro: "Retinoid" is an umbrella term. In cosmetic products you will most commonly see the following forms, listed from most biologically active to least:
body.familyTretinoin: <bold>Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid, ATRA).</bold> Prescription only in most jurisdictions. Directly binds retinoic acid receptors (RAR). Not permitted in OTC cosmetics in the EU or US.
body.familyAdapalene: <bold>Adapalene.</bold> A synthetic third-generation retinoid. OTC in the US since 2016 (Differin 0.1%). Prescription in most of the EU.
body.familyHpr: <bold>Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR, Granactive Retinoid).</bold> An ester of retinoic acid that binds RAR directly without prior conversion. Cosmetic-grade.
body.familyRetinaldehyde: <bold>Retinaldehyde (retinal).</bold> One metabolic step away from retinoic acid. More potent than retinol. Cosmetic-grade.
body.familyRetinol: <bold>Retinol.</bold> The canonical cosmetic retinoid. Converted intracellularly: retinol → retinaldehyde → retinoic acid. Cosmetic concentrations typically 0.1–1%.
body.familyEsters: <bold>Retinyl palmitate / retinyl acetate / retinyl propionate.</bold> Retinol esters. The weakest forms — two metabolic steps from activity. Stable, well-tolerated, but require significantly higher concentrations to match retinol efficacy.
body.evidenceP1: The landmark placebo-controlled trial on cosmetic retinol remains Kafi et al. (2007): 0.4% retinol vs vehicle, 36 elderly subjects (80+), 24 weeks, applied three times per week. Statistically significant improvements in fine wrinkles and overall photoaging [1].
body.evidenceP2: For retinaldehyde, Diridollou et al. (1999) showed that 0.05% retinaldehyde over 18 weeks significantly reduced wrinkle depth and roughness, with tolerance superior to tretinoin in head-to-head comparisons <sup>[2]</sup>.
body.evidenceP3: Retinyl palmitate — the form that shows up most often in drugstore moisturisers — has markedly weaker evidence. A 2011 meta-analysis concluded that efficacy data for retinyl esters in photoaging are limited and inconsistent [3].
body.pregnancyIntro: This is the most important section of this article. Oral isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid, Accutane) is a confirmed human teratogen — the FDA iPLEDGE program exists specifically because of this. The critical question for cosmetics is: do topical retinoids cross the placenta in meaningful quantities?
body.systemicP1: A 2015 systematic review of topical retinoid exposure during pregnancy found that no statistically significant increase in major congenital malformations has been demonstrated from topical tretinoin, adapalene, or retinol use in human case series [4]. The biological plausibility of teratogenicity at topical cosmetic concentrations is low — stratum corneum absorption of retinol esters in particular is minimal.
body.systemicP2: <bold>But.</bold> Case reports of retinoid embryopathy following topical tretinoin exposure exist, and the EMA and FDA both maintain a formal precautionary warning. The benefit/risk calculus for an elective cosmetic ingredient during pregnancy is unambiguous: <bold>avoid</bold>. There is no medical reason to use a cosmetic retinoid during pregnancy, and there are multiple equally effective alternatives (niacinamide, bakuchiol, peptides).
body.calloutDefaultBody: Any retinoid INCI name — RETINOL, RETINYL PALMITATE, RETINAL, HYDROXYPINACOLONE RETINOATE, ADAPALENE, TRETINOIN, RETINYL ACETATE, RETINYL PROPIONATE — returns pregnancySafe: false and the product's pregnancy safety report flags the ingredient explicitly. This is a conservative default aligned with EMA and FDA guidance.
body.euRegIntro: In 2024, the EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) adopted Opinion SCCS/1639/21 restricting retinol, retinyl acetate, and retinyl palmitate:
body.euRegLeaveOn: Face/hand leave-on products: max <bold>0.05%</bold> retinol equivalent (RE).
body.euRegWarning: Warning label required on pack: "Contains retinol. Avoid exposure during pregnancy" (exact wording per the amending regulation).
body.euRegOutro: These limits took effect for new products placed on the market in November 2025, with phase-out through May 2027. Products sold in the EU must comply. INCI API returns the EU maximum concentration in euMaxConcentration for each retinoid form.
body.usRegBody: Retinyl palmitate and retinol are permitted in cosmetics. Tretinoin is prescription. There is no federal concentration cap on cosmetic retinol, but the California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) added retinol and retinyl palmitate to the Prop 65 list in 2016 for developmental toxicity — triggering warning labels on products sold in California above the no-significant-risk level.
body.irritationP1: Retinoids universally trigger some level of irritation during the first 2–6 weeks of use ("retinization"): dryness, peeling, tingling, and temporary erythema. This is a pharmacological effect, not an allergic reaction, and it subsides as the epidermis adapts.
body.irritationP2: Retinoids increase sun sensitivity in two ways: by thinning the stratum corneum initially, and because retinoic acid itself is photodegraded. Daily SPF 30+ is a non-negotiable part of any retinoid protocol. INCI API returns photosensitivityRisk: "high" for active retinoids and "moderate" for the retinol esters.
body.stackingTitle: What not to stack with retinoids
body.stackingAha: <bold>AHAs/BHAs at the same step.</bold> Combined exfoliation and retinoid use increases irritation sharply. Alternate nights.
body.stackingBpo: <bold>Benzoyl peroxide.</bold> Oxidises tretinoin and retinol directly. Use at different times of day if combining for acne.
body.stackingVitC: <bold>Vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid).</bold> Not dangerous, but the pH requirements conflict — use AM vitamin C, PM retinoid.
body.calloutRunBody: GET /v1/ingredients/retinol/full and GET /v1/products/:barcode/pregnancy both return the retinoid pregnancy flag described here, plus source attribution.

eu-allergens-2023-1545.title: EU Fragrance Allergens — From 26 to 80+ Under Regulation 2023/1545
eu-allergens-2023-1545.excerpt: A developer guide to EU Regulation 2023/1545: the 56 newly disclosable fragrance allergens, transition timelines (July 2026 / July 2028), and how INCI API flags them automatically.
eu-allergens-2023-1545.heroLead: In July 2023 the EU tripled the mandatory fragrance allergen list. Every label in Europe is being rewritten. Here is what that means for your app.

body.intro: On 26 July 2023, the EU Commission published <regLink>Regulation (EU) 2023/1545</regLink>, amending Annex III of Cosmetic Regulation 1223/2009. In one stroke it tripled the mandatory fragrance allergen disclosure list — from the familiar 26 substances to 82 individual entries. Every cosmetic product sold in the European Union is being relabelled. This is a developer guide to what changed, what the transition timeline looks like, and how INCI API handles it.
body.beforeTitle: What the old list looked like
body.beforeBody: Since 2005, EU Cosmetic Regulation had required on-pack disclosure of 26 specific fragrance allergens when present above concentration thresholds (0.001% in leave-on, 0.01% in rinse-off). These included the usual suspects: linalool, limonene, citronellol, geraniol, eugenol, and so on. If your product contained them above threshold, they had to appear by name in the INCI list — not hidden behind the generic Parfum / Fragrance label.
body.changedIntro: The regulation added <bold>56 new individually named allergens</bold> to the disclosure list, reflecting 20 years of accumulated Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) evidence on fragrance sensitisation. Highlights include:
body.changedComponents: <bold>Common essential oil components</bold> now named individually rather than buried in "Parfum": acetylcedrene, acetylhexamethyl tetralin, amylcinnamaldehyde, benzaldehyde, camphor, carvone, β-caryophyllene, α-damascone, δ-damascone, α-ionone, β-ionone, methyleugenol, menthol, p-mentha-1,8-dien-7-al (perillaldehyde), rose ketone 4, salicylaldehyde, terpinolene, terpineol, vanillin.
body.changedExtracts: <bold>Specific plant extracts</bold> with natural allergen content: cananga odorata extract, cedrus atlantica bark oil, cinnamomum cassia leaf oil, cinnamomum zeylanicum bark extract/oil, citrus aurantium amara extracts, citrus limon peel oil, cymbopogon citratus/schoenanthus oils, eucalyptus globulus oils, eugenia caryophyllus oils, jasminum officinale/grandiflorum extracts, juniperus virginiana oil, laurus nobilis oil, lavandula hybrida oil, mentha piperita/spicata oil, narcissus poeticus extract, pelargonium graveolens oils, pogostemon cablin oil, rose flower oil/extract, santalum album oil, turpentine.
body.timeline1: 31 July 2026 — products placed on the EU market from this date must have compliant labelling. Non-compliant stock produced before this date may continue to flow through distribution.
body.timeline2: <bold>31 July 2028</bold> — hard end. All products on EU shelves, including previously-placed stock, must bear compliant labels. Non-compliant products must be withdrawn.
body.calloutDatesBody: The July 2026 deadline hits producers (new SKUs, new batches). The July 2028 deadline hits retailers and distributors (any product still on shelf). Compliance teams plan for both.
body.concentrationsIntro: Same as before: individual allergen names must appear in the INCI list when their concentration in the finished product exceeds:
body.concentrationsOutro: Below these thresholds, the allergen can still be covered by the generic Parfum or Aroma declaration. No change.
body.impactLength: INCI lists will get significantly longer. A 30-word INCI before the amendment may be a 45-word INCI after, because individual fragrance components that previously lived inside Parfum now have to appear by name.
body.impactFlags: <bold>Allergen flags per product will rise.</bold> Products that previously showed "2 EU allergens detected" may now show 5–7, because the underlying formulation didn't change — disclosure did.
body.impactCopy: Consumer-facing language matters. An "EU allergen" in this regulatory sense is a substance regulators require to be declared. It is not a diagnosis of allergy. Most consumers will not react to any given listed allergen. Your UI should word these flags carefully.
body.apiTitle: How INCI API handles the change
body.detectionBody: Our cosmetic_ingredients collection carries the full 2023/1545 list tagged with isEuAllergen: true. New INCI names added to the list went live in our database on the date of regulation publication — your integrations were flagging them 3 years before the first compliance deadline.
body.endpointsAllergens: GET /v1/products/:barcode/allergens returns the full current EU allergen report for a product, including both pre-2023 and post-2023 additions.
body.endpointsIngredient: GET /v1/ingredients/:inciName includes isEuAllergen, allergenTypes (fragrance, preservative, dye, contact), and regulatorySource attributing the specific regulation or annex entry.
body.endpointsAnalyze: POST /v1/analyze accepts a raw INCI string and returns the allergen count and list without requiring a barcode.
body.developerTitle: What to ship in your app
body.developer1: Display the allergen count prominently, but show the individual allergen list only on demand. Long lists without context alarm users.
body.developer2: Pair the list with sensible copy: "X substances that EU regulations require to be disclosed on the label. This does not mean they are unsafe — most people can use them without issue."
body.developer3: If your app is for a specific market, filter. Linalool flagging in an EU app is useful. The same flag in a product sold only in Japan is less actionable — Japan has its own labelling rules. INCI API returns regulatoryRegions: ["EU"] so you can scope appropriately.
body.developer4: If your users can declare their own known allergies, intersect that list against the ingredient's CAS number, not its INCI name. INCI names have synonyms ("Hexyl cinnamal" vs "Hexyl cinnamic aldehyde"); CAS numbers don't.
body.calloutFurtherBody: The full legal text is on EUR-Lex: <regLink>Regulation (EU) 2023/1545</regLink>. The underlying SCCS opinions are published on the <sccsLink>European Commission Health website</sccsLink>.

Replace months of ingredient research with one API call. Safety scoring, allergen detection, skin compatibility, and pregnancy safety in a single endpoint.

Every ingredient rated 1-10 based on EU CosIng, CIR, and published research.

EU 80 mandatory allergens + contact sensitizers + preservative allergens flagged instantly.

Flag retinoids, BHAs, and other pregnancy-unsafe ingredients automatically.

Every effect backed by RCT or peer-reviewed evidence — see mechanism, biomarker, and clinical concentration.

cta.title: ¿Listo para añadir inteligencia de ingredientes a tu app?
cta.subtitle: Únete a los desarrolladores de apps de belleza que confían en INCI API para puntuación de seguridad cosmética, detección de alérgenos y análisis de compatibilidad cutánea. Gratis para todos ahora: 20 000 solicitudes al mes.

0.a: INCI API es una API de inteligencia de ingredientes cosméticos que permite a los desarrolladores buscar productos de belleza por código de barras y obtener un análisis INCI completo (Nomenclatura Internacional de Ingredientes Cosméticos), incluyendo puntuaciones de seguridad, detección de alérgenos, compatibilidad cutánea, seguridad durante el embarazo y puntuaciones de clean beauty. Es la capa de infraestructura para aplicaciones de belleza, planificadores de rutinas de skincare y plataformas de comercio electrónico de cosméticos.

1.q: ¿Cómo funciona el análisis de ingredientes por código de barras?
1.a: Envía un código UPC o EAN al endpoint de INCI API. La API identifica el producto, extrae la lista INCI completa y procesa cada ingrediente con nuestro motor de análisis. Recibes puntuaciones de seguridad (1-10), alertas de alérgenos, índices de comedogenicidad, compatibilidad por tipo de piel y seguridad durante el embarazo — todo en una sola respuesta JSON en menos de 100 ms.

2.a: Sí, INCI API ofrece un nivel gratuito con 100 solicitudes al mes que incluye información básica del producto y la lista INCI. Los planes de pago comienzan en 9 $/mes con 5.000 solicitudes, puntuaciones de seguridad y detección de alérgenos. No se requiere tarjeta de crédito para el plan gratuito.

3.q: ¿Qué datos incluye la puntuación de seguridad?
3.a: La puntuación de seguridad es una valoración ponderada de 1 a 10 por ingrediente, basada en la base de datos EU CosIng, los informes CIR (Cosmetic Ingredient Review) e investigaciones dermatológicas publicadas. La puntuación general del producto también incluye una puntuación de clean beauty (0-100), índice de comedogenicidad (0-5) y una ponderación por posición que refleja la concentración.

4.q: ¿Qué bases de datos cosméticas utiliza INCI API?
4.a: INCI API agrega datos de EU CosIng (30.000+ ingredientes, CC BY 4.0), Open Beauty Facts (200.000+ productos cosméticos, ODbL), Reglamento UE 1223/2009 y 2023/1545 para alérgenos, escala de comedogenicidad de Fulton 1989 y revisiones de seguridad CIR. La base de datos incluye 82 alérgenos UE, 103 valoraciones de comedogenicidad y 21 ingredientes no seguros durante el embarazo.

5.q: ¿Puedo analizar ingredientes sin un código de barras?
5.a: Sí. El endpoint POST /v1/analyze acepta una lista INCI sin procesar y devuelve el análisis completo sin necesidad de código de barras. Está disponible en los planes Pro y Business y es ideal para herramientas de formulación, apps de escaneo de etiquetas o verificadores de ingredientes.

6.a: INCI API detecta los 80+ alérgenos obligatorios de la UE definidos en el Reglamento 1223/2009 y la actualización 2023/1545, incluyendo alérgenos de fragancia como Linalool, Limoneno y Citronelol. También señala sensibilizantes de contacto, alérgenos conservantes y alérgenos colorantes con grados de severidad.

7.q: ¿Es la API adecuada para aplicaciones de belleza comerciales?
7.a: Absolutamente. INCI API está diseñada como infraestructura para aplicaciones de belleza comerciales. Con un 99,9 % de tiempo activo, tiempos de respuesta inferiores a 100 ms y planes que escalan hasta 100.000 solicitudes/mes, alimenta apps de skincare, escáneres de ingredientes, e-commerce de belleza y motores de recomendación cosmética. what.title: ¿Qué es INCI? Una guía rápida sobre los ingredientes cosméticos
what.p1: INCI (Nomenclatura Internacional de Ingredientes Cosméticos) es el sistema estandarizado para nombrar ingredientes cosméticos en todo el mundo. Establecido por la UE y adoptado globalmente, los nombres INCI aparecen en cada etiqueta cosmética para que los consumidores puedan identificar exactamente qué se aplican en la piel.
what.p2: Los ingredientes siempre se listan en orden descendente de concentración: los primeros constituyen la mayor parte de la fórmula. Los ingredientes presentes en menos del 1% pueden listarse en cualquier orden. Esto significa que los primeros 5-6 ingredientes suelen representar el 80% o más del producto.
what.p3: Entender tu lista INCI es clave para tomar decisiones informadas sobre tu rutina de cuidado de la piel, maquillaje y productos de belleza. Nuestro verificador gratuito analiza cada ingrediente con bases de datos de confianza como EU CosIng, los informes de seguridad CIR y el Reglamento UE 1223/2009.

0.name: Parabenos
0.why: Posibles disruptores endocrinos. Busca: Methylparaben, Propylparaben, Butylparaben.

1.name: Formaldehído y liberadores
1.why: Carcinógeno conocido. Presente en: DMDM Hydantoin, Imidazolidinyl Urea.

2.name: Lauril sulfato de sodio (SLS)
2.why: Tensioactivo agresivo que puede irritar la piel y los ojos.

3.name: Oxibenzona
3.why: Filtro UV vinculado a alteraciones hormonales y daño a los arrecifes de coral.

4.name: Triclosán
4.why: Agente antibacteriano vinculado a la resistencia a antibióticos y efectos hormonales.

5.name: Retinoides (en el embarazo)
5.why: Retinol, palmitato de retinilo: seguros normalmente, pero no durante el embarazo.

6.name: Ftalatos
6.why: Plastificantes a menudo ocultos bajo «Fragancia», vinculados a alteraciones endocrinas.

7.name: Fragancias sintéticas
7.why: Pueden contener cientos de sustancias químicas no declaradas; desencadenante alérgico común.

8.name: BHA/BHT
8.why: Conservantes con posibles propiedades disruptoras endocrinas.

9.name: Colorantes de alquitrán de hulla
9.why: Vinculados a riesgo de cáncer. Busca números CI y nombres de colores FD&C.

0.q: ¿Cómo compruebo si mi cosmético es seguro?
0.a: Encuentra la lista de ingredientes (INCI) en el envase de tu producto, normalmente en la etiqueta posterior. Copia la lista completa y pégala en nuestro verificador. Analizaremos cada ingrediente con la base de datos EU CosIng, identificaremos alérgenos, marcaremos los no seguros durante el embarazo y te daremos una puntuación general de seguridad de 0 a 100.

1.a: INCI significa Nomenclatura Internacional de Ingredientes Cosméticos. Es el sistema de nomenclatura estandarizado usado en todo el mundo para listar ingredientes en cosméticos y productos de cuidado personal. Por ley (Reglamento UE 1223/2009), todos los cosméticos vendidos en la UE deben listar los ingredientes con nombres INCI en orden descendente de concentración.

2.q: ¿Cómo se calcula la puntuación de seguridad?
2.a: Nuestra puntuación de seguridad (0-100) se calcula analizando cada ingrediente con investigaciones publicadas de la base de datos EU CosIng, los informes CIR (Cosmetic Ingredient Review) y el Reglamento UE 1223/2009. Cada ingrediente recibe una calificación de riesgo (1-10) y calculamos un promedio ponderado por orden de concentración (los primeros están presentes en mayores cantidades). La puntuación de belleza limpia penaliza adicionalmente parabenos, SLS, liberadores de formaldehído y PEG.

3.a: Los parabenos (Methylparaben, Propylparaben, etc.) son conservantes con leves propiedades imitadoras de estrógenos. La UE los permite en cosméticos a concentraciones restringidas (hasta 0,4% para parabenos individuales). Aunque el Comité Científico de la UE los considera seguros a niveles regulados, muchos consumidores prefieren evitarlos. Nuestro verificador los marca como ingredientes de nivel «precaución».

4.q: ¿Qué ingredientes debo evitar durante el embarazo?
4.a: Durante el embarazo, los dermatólogos recomiendan evitar: retinoides (retinol, palmitato de retinilo, tretinoína), ácido salicílico (BHA) en altas concentraciones, hidroquinona, ftalatos, triclosán, oxibenzona y filtros solares químicos. Nuestro verificador marca automáticamente los 21 ingredientes conocidos como no seguros durante el embarazo cuando los detecta en tu producto.
